rationale: A wins because it finds the harder second-order story, not just the launch wrapper: "Plaid needs 12,000 banks to help route payments past the fees banks collect" is the kind of tension a real beat reporter can interrogate. B has usable bones, especially "Flat fee vs. interchange: the math behind Plaid's \"up to 70% cheaper\" claim," but it mostly stops at the obvious three lanes and does less to arm the founder for the first hostile follow-up. A is the one I would hand to a founder before calls; B still needs another pass from someone who has been yelled at by a payments reporter.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow adoption stories have mostly been about disbursements and B2B" imports outside market context that was not in the update. Good instinct, but mark it as something to verify, not a supplied fact.
"The 70% saving only shows up on big-ticket sales" overstates the fact. The update says the claim is "up to 70% lower" on large transactions; "only" needs the break-even math first.
"the fees banks collect" is a strong headline but still an inference from card economics, not a supplied fact. A later note admits this, but the headline should not get ahead of the proof.
gaps_in_B: "merchant-facing on-ramp through Plaid's 12,000 bank connections" risks conflating Plaid connectivity with FedNow payment reach. The update does not say all 12,000 institutions can transact over FedNow.

"a fintech or banking trade outlet" is serviceable but soft. It needs the tighter sub-beat discipline A had: merchant acquiring, acceptance cost, real-time payments infrastructure, bank payments revenue.

"at least one merchant or processing-volume detail beyond \"early merchants\"" is too permissive. A processing-volume detail is not a substitute for a named merchant when the whole story is merchant savings.

B misses two brutal questions that would change the pitch: bank-side revenue tension and "Who eats fraud and disputes?" Those are not decorative; they decide whether this is a serious payments story or product-copy fog.
